intro: Many people picture Satan as a horned monster and think of demons as the stuff of scary movies. The ancient texts are quieter and more interesting than that. In the Hebrew Bible, satan is a word for an adversary. In Job, "the satan" stands in God's own court. Much later, the New Testament uses Satan and the devil as names for one enemy of God. This unit follows how that change happened.

This unit reads the documents first. They include the Hebrew Bible, the Greek Septuagint, 1 Enoch and Jubilees, the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Gospels. Early Christian writers such as Justin Martyr and Origen join them. Then you meet the researchers who study these texts. Among them are Peggy Day, Elaine Pagels, Archie T. Wright, Walter Wink and Michael Heiser. You will read each view beside Jewish and Christian readings.

By the end of the unit you will be able to explain what satan means in Hebrew and why the word "the" matters. You will compare readings of Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28. You will trace names like Belial and Mastema, read 1 Enoch 15 and the Gospel stories in Mark, and explain the two goats of the Day of Atonement. You will also practice reading these stories with care.
bigQuestion: How did ancient texts picture the powers that stand against God, and how have readers explained where they came from?

timeline.t: Isaiah begins to prophesy in Jerusalem; Isaiah 14 later mocks the king of Babylon
Ezekiel's lament pictures the king of Tyre as a being cast out of Eden
Zechariah sees the satan accusing Joshua the high priest
The Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1–36) tells of the giants' spirits
Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, the Septuagint, begins
The book of Jubilees names Mastema as chief of the spirits
Copies of the War Scroll, found at Qumran, describe Belial and the sons of darkness
Jesus teaches in Galilee and frees people from unclean spirits, as the Gospels tell
Revelation 12:9 calls the dragon the old serpent, the devil and Satan
Justin Martyr writes that demons are the children of angels and women
William Tyndale coins the English word scapegoat for Leviticus 16
J. T. Milik publishes the Aramaic fragments of 1 Enoch from Qumran Cave 4

words.d: a Hebrew word meaning adversary; "the satan" in Job and Zechariah is an accuser in God's court
scholars' term for God's heavenly court of spirit beings, as in Job 1 and Psalm 82
the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun around the 200s BCE
from the Greek diabolos, slanderer; in the New Testament, a name for Satan
the Hebrew word for the serpent in Genesis 3
Latin for the morning star; the KJV's word in Isaiah 14:12 for the king of Babylon
from a Hebrew word for worthlessness; in the Dead Sea Scrolls, the leader of evil
from a Hebrew word for hostility; the chief of the spirits in Jubilees
rulers; in Paul's letters, spiritual powers that many scholars link to the sons of God over the nations
the Gospels' phrase for a demon; unclean means not fit to come near God's holy presence

test.q: What does the Hebrew word satan mean?
test.why: Satan is a Hebrew word for an adversary or opponent, used for angels, kings and soldiers.

test.q: Why do many scholars read "the satan" in Job as a title, not a name?
choices: It is written in Greek letters
It appears only in the Septuagint
It has the article "the", which names usually do not take
test.why: The Hebrew has the article ha-: "the satan" describes a role, as "the judge" does. Peggy Day and others make this point.

test.q: Who does the satan accuse in Zechariah 3?
test.why: Zechariah 3:1 shows the satan at the right hand of Joshua the high priest, accusing him.

test.q: Which poem is addressed to the king of Tyre?
test.why: Ezekiel 28 is a lament over the king of Tyre, who is pictured in Eden. Isaiah 14 is about the king of Babylon.

test.q: What did Heiser see behind Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28?
choices: Human kings pictured through the story of the Eden rebel
The spirits of the dead giants
test.why: Heiser read both poems as aimed at real kings but patterned on the story of a divine rebel cast down from Eden.

test.q: Which Greek word gave English the word devil?
test.why: Devil comes from diabolos, slanderer, which the Septuagint used for ha-satan in Job.

test.q: In which book is Mastema the chief of the spirits?
test.why: Jubilees, from about 160 BCE, names Mastema as chief of the evil spirits.

test.q: Which verse gathers the names dragon, old serpent, devil and Satan?
test.why: Revelation 12:9 gives all four names for one figure who deceives the whole world.

test.q: Which early Christian writer said demons were the children of angels and women?
test.why: Justin Martyr, in his Second Apology (c. 150 CE), wrote that the angels' children with women are the ones called demons.

test.q: What does 1 Enoch 15 say about the giants' spirits?
choices: They became evil spirits living on the earth
They were sent away on the Day of Atonement
They became the rulers of the nations
test.why: 1 Enoch 15:8–12 says the spirits that came out of the dead giants became evil spirits on the earth.

test.q: Which Hebrew word in Deuteronomy 32:17 names spirit beings Israel sacrificed to?
test.why: Deuteronomy 32:17 uses shedim, which the Septuagint translated as demons.

test.q: How does Mark 5 end for the man from the tombs?
choices: He follows Jesus by boat to Capernaum
He goes home and tells his story in the Ten Cities
test.why: In Mark 5:19–20 Jesus sends the man home to his friends, and he tells his story in the Decapolis.

test.q: How do the Gospels treat healing the sick and freeing people from spirits?
choices: As things only priests could do
As things that never happened in Galilee
As two separate things, as in Mark 1:32–34
test.why: Mark 1:32–34 lists the sick and those troubled by demons as two groups, keeping healing and freeing apart.

test.q: What happened to the goat for Azazel on the Day of Atonement?
choices: It carried the people's sins into the wilderness
It was given to the high priest's family
It was kept in the temple courtyard
It was offered on the altar
test.why: Leviticus 16:21–22 says the high priest confessed the sins over the living goat, and it was led into the wilderness.

test.q: Which view says demons are fallen angels who followed Satan?
choices: Justin Martyr's view of the angels' children
A common Christian view drawing on Revelation 12:9
test.why: Many Christians teach that demons are angels who joined Satan, pointing to Revelation 12:9. Justin Martyr and 1 Enoch saw them as the giants' spirits.

write.prompt: Where did ancient readers think the Bible's dark powers came from? Choose two or three passages from this unit, such as Job 1:6, Isaiah 14:12, 1 Enoch 15:8–12 or Mark 5:1–20. Explain what each text says first. Then explain how at least two readers have read it, such as Origen, Justin Martyr, the Talmud, Heiser or many Christian readers, and where they differ.
tips: Start from the document: say what the text says before you give any reading of it.
Name each text you cite with its book, chapter and verse.
Attribute every idea: "Justin Martyr wrote…", "Heiser argued…", "many Jewish readers see…".
Compare the readings fairly; you do not need to pick a winner.
Use the unit's terms, such as satan, divine council, Watchers and unclean spirit, and explain each one.

title: The Satan, Demons and Dark Powers

chapters.title: The Satan, the Serpent and the Devil
chapters.bigQuestion: How did a Hebrew word for "adversary" become the name of the Bible's great enemy of God?

story.title: Who Let Him In?
story.kicker: A student reading Job notices something odd: the satan walks into God's court as if he belongs there.
paragraphs: Maya had a reading assignment for her literature class: the first two chapters of the book of Job. She expected a simple story about a good man who suffers. She opened a Bible at her kitchen table in Joliet and started to read. By the sixth verse she had stopped and read the line again.

The story says the sons of God came to stand before the LORD. It sounds like a royal court, with officials reporting to their king. Then the text says the satan came along with them. Nobody throws him out. Nobody seems surprised. God even speaks to him first and asks where he has been.

Maya had always pictured Satan as a monster with horns, far from God. This figure seemed different. He talked like an official doing a job. He questioned whether Job was good only because life had been easy for him. God set limits on what he could do, and he obeyed them.

She showed her older brother, who was taking a course on the Hebrew Bible. He pointed to a small note at the bottom of the page. It said the Hebrew has "the satan", with the word "the", and that the word means adversary. "So is it a name or a job title?" Maya asked. Her brother smiled. "Scholars have written whole books on that question."

Scholars have followed that question a long way. Peggy L. Day studied every use of the Hebrew word in An Adversary in Heaven (1988). Elaine Pagels traced the later story in The Origin of Satan (1995). This chapter follows the path through the ancient texts themselves. It starts with a word for an opponent. It ends with the names Satan and the devil in the New Testament.
story.think: Why might a small word like "the" change how a reader understands who a character is?

lessons.title: What Satan Means
lessons.mainIdea: In Hebrew, satan is an ordinary word that means adversary, someone who opposes or blocks another.
reading: Start with Numbers 22. A foreign prophet named Balaam rides his donkey toward Moab. The text says the angel of the LORD stood in the road "as an adversary" against him. The Hebrew word there is *satan*. Here the adversary is God's own messenger. He blocks the road to stop Balaam from doing wrong.

The same word is used for people. In 1 Samuel 29:4, Philistine commanders worry that David might become a satan against them in battle. In 1 Kings 11:14, God raises up Hadad the Edomite as a satan against King Solomon. In these verses the word just means an enemy or opponent. Nobody in them is a spirit being.

So satan in the Hebrew Bible is first a common noun, like the English word "opponent". It describes a role, not one fixed person. Anyone can be a satan to someone else: a soldier, a king or an angel. Scholars call this the word's plain *meaning*, and it is the starting point for everything else in this chapter.

Peggy L. Day made this point in An Adversary in Heaven (1988). She studied each place the Hebrew Bible uses the word. She argued that it does not yet name one single enemy of God there. Many scholars share her starting point. First ask who is opposing whom in each passage.

words.d: a Hebrew word meaning adversary or opponent; someone who stands against another
what a word says in its own language and setting, before later ideas are added

look.title: Four Adversaries
look.text: Numbers 22:22 — the angel of the LORD stands in the road as a satan against Balaam. 1 Samuel 29:4 — the Philistines fear David may be a satan against them. 1 Kings 11:14 — Hadad the Edomite is a satan against Solomon. Job 1:6 — the satan comes before the LORD with the sons of God.
look.prompt: In the first three verses, who is the adversary and who is being opposed? Which of the four seems different, and why?

check.q: What does the Hebrew word satan mean?
check.why: Satan is a Hebrew word for an adversary, someone who opposes another. Serpent is nachash and messenger is mal'ak.

check.q: In Numbers 22:22, who stands in the road as a satan against Balaam?
check.why: Numbers 22:22 says the angel of the LORD stood in the road as an adversary to block Balaam.

check.q: What did Peggy L. Day study in An Adversary in Heaven (1988)?
choices: The poems about the king of Tyre only
The uses of the word satan in the Hebrew Bible
The Greek words of the Gospel of Mark
The War Scroll from the Dead Sea
check.why: Day's 1988 book looked at each use of satan in the Hebrew Bible. She argued the word does not yet name one single enemy of God there.

lessons.title: The Satan in God's Court
lessons.mainIdea: In Job 1–2 the satan is a member of God's heavenly court who questions whether Job serves God for nothing.
reading: Job 1:6 opens a heavenly scene. The sons of God come to present themselves before the LORD, and the satan comes among them. In Hebrew the word has the article: ha-satan, "the satan". Many scholars read this as a title, like "the prosecutor" or "the challenger".

The setting is what scholars call the *divine council*: God's heavenly court, where spirit beings stand before him. In Job, the satan reports that he has been roaming the earth. God points to Job as a man without equal. The satan answers that Job is good only because God protects him and his family.

God allows a test, but sets clear limits. In chapter 1 the satan may not touch Job himself. In chapter 2 he may not take Job's life. The satan can only act inside the bounds God gives. After chapter 2 he never appears in the book again.

Many modern scholars argue that this satan is not the devil of later writings. They see an officer of the court doing a hard job, perhaps with a bad attitude. Many Christian readers have long read Job's satan as the devil himself. Both readings look closely at the same two chapters.

words.d: scholars' term for God's heavenly court, the spirit beings who stand before God in texts like Job 1 and Psalm 82
a small word like "the"; in Hebrew it is attached to the front of a noun (ha-)
a Hebrew phrase for heavenly beings who serve in God's court

look.title: The Court Scene
look.text: Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan came also among them.
look.prompt: The King James Version prints "Satan" as a name, while the Hebrew says "the satan". How might each choice shape what a reader pictures?

check.q: In Job 1:6, who comes before the LORD along with the satan?
check.why: Job 1:6 says the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and the satan came among them.

check.q: What limit does God set on the satan in Job 2?
choices: He may not speak to God again
He may not visit Job's friends
He may not take Job's life
check.why: In Job 2 God allows the satan to touch Job's body but not to take his life.

check.q: How do many modern scholars read the satan in Job?
choices: As one of Job's three friends
As a human judge in Job's town
As the king of Tyre in disguise
As an officer in God's court, not the later devil
check.why: Many scholars read ha-satan in Job as a council member acting as a challenger. Many Christian readers see the devil there instead.

lessons.title: An Accuser in Zechariah
lessons.mainIdea: In Zechariah 3 the satan accuses the high priest Joshua, and the LORD rebukes the accuser.
reading: Zechariah was a prophet in Jerusalem around 520 BCE. His people had come back from exile in Babylon and were rebuilding the temple. In Zechariah 3 he sees a vision set in a heavenly court. Joshua the high priest stands before the angel of the LORD. The satan stands at his right hand to *accuse* him.

Joshua is wearing filthy clothes. In the vision, that dirt pictures the people's guilt. The satan's job seems to be to point it out. But the accuser does not get the last word. The LORD rebukes the satan and calls Joshua a burning stick snatched from the fire.
Then the dirty clothes are taken off. Joshua is given clean robes and a clean turban. The vision says his guilt has been taken away. The scene moves from accusation to cleansing and a fresh start.

Like Job, this text uses the article: ha-satan. Scholars point out that in both books the satan acts inside God's court, as an accuser. In both, God has the final say. Readers have noticed that the accuser in Zechariah ends up rebuked, a step toward the enemy of God pictured in later writings.

words.d: to charge someone with doing wrong, as a prosecutor does in court
the chief priest of Israel's temple, who led its worship

look.title: Dirty Clothes, Clean Robes
look.text: Paraphrase of Zechariah 3:1–5: Joshua the high priest stands before the angel of the LORD in dirty clothes. The satan stands at his side to accuse him. The LORD rebukes the satan. The dirty clothes are removed, and Joshua is dressed in clean robes and a clean turban.
look.prompt: What do the clothes stand for in this vision? What happens to the accuser's case by the end?

check.q: What is the satan doing in Zechariah 3?
choices: Standing at Joshua's side to accuse him
Guarding the gate of the temple
Leading the people back from Babylon
check.why: Zechariah 3:1 shows the satan standing at the right hand of Joshua the high priest to accuse him.

check.q: What happens to Joshua's dirty clothes in the vision?
choices: They are burned on the altar
They are replaced with clean robes
They are given to the satan
They are buried in the ground
check.why: In Zechariah 3:4–5 the dirty clothes are taken away and Joshua is dressed in clean robes, a sign his guilt is removed.

check.q: What do Job 1–2 and Zechariah 3 have in common?
choices: Both describe the king of Tyre
Both are set in the garden of Eden
Both say "the satan", an accuser in God's court
check.why: Both texts use ha-satan, with the article, for an accuser who acts inside God's heavenly court.

lessons.title: Why "The" Matters
lessons.mainIdea: Job and Zechariah say "the satan", which works like a title for a role, not the personal name it becomes in the New Testament.
reading: In Hebrew, as in English, people's names usually do not take "the". Nobody says "the Moses" or "the Sarah". But Job and Zechariah say "the satan". Heiser argued in Demons (2020) that this small word is a clue. It shows the word is working as a *title*, a description of a role, not a *proper name*.

Think of "the judge" or "the coach". Those words tell you what a person does, not who the person is. Heiser read ha-satan the same way: the one whose job was to challenge. This is why he said the Old Testament does not use satan as a name the way the New Testament uses Satan.

One verse is harder. In 1 Chronicles 21:1 the word appears without "the": satan stood up against Israel and moved David to count the people. Many translations print it as the name Satan. Other scholars translate "an adversary", which could mean a human enemy or an unnamed spirit. The retelling of the same story in 2 Samuel 24:1 says the LORD's anger moved David.

Readers handle this in different ways. Some see the Chronicler naming the devil for the first time. Others doubt the verse gives a personal name. The debate shows how much one small word can matter when reading ancient texts.

words.d: a word that names a role or job, such as "the judge"
a word that names one particular person or place, such as Moses or Jerusalem

look.title: Same Story, Two Tellings
look.text: Paraphrase of 2 Samuel 24:1: The LORD's anger burned against Israel, and he moved David to count the people. Paraphrase of 1 Chronicles 21:1: Satan (or "an adversary") stood up against Israel and moved David to count the people.
look.prompt: The two books tell the same event. What changes between them? Why might translators disagree about whether to write "Satan" or "an adversary"?

check.q: Why did Heiser think "the satan" in Job is a title?
choices: Job calls him by his first name
The word only appears in Greek
Hebrew names usually do not take "the"
The word is written in red ink
check.why: Heiser argued that the article "the" shows a role being described, since personal names normally do not take it.

check.q: Which verse uses the word without "the" and is debated?
check.why: 1 Chronicles 21:1 has satan without the article, so scholars debate whether it is the name Satan or "an adversary".

check.q: According to 2 Samuel 24:1, what moved David to count the people?
check.why: 2 Samuel 24:1 says the LORD's anger burned against Israel and moved David. 1 Chronicles 21:1 tells the same event with satan.

lessons.title: From Satan to Devil
lessons.mainIdea: Greek translators turned satan into diabolos, "slanderer", which gave English the word devil.
reading: Around the 200s BCE, Jewish scholars began to translate the Hebrew Bible into Greek. That translation is called the *Septuagint*. In Job, the translators wrote ho diabolos for ha-satan. Diabolos means slanderer, someone who speaks lies or accusations against another. Brenton's English version of the Septuagint (1844) reads Job 1:6 as "the devil came with them".

The English word *devil* comes from diabolos. So does the Spanish diablo. When the New Testament was written in Greek, its writers used both words. Sometimes they wrote Satanas, the Hebrew word in Greek letters. Sometimes they wrote diabolos. By then both had become names for one enemy of God.

Revelation 12:9 pulls the names together in one line. It calls one figure the great dragon, the old serpent, the devil and Satan, who deceives the whole world. Scholars often point to this verse. It links the serpent of Eden with Satan and the devil, something the Old Testament never spells out.

So the path runs like this. A Hebrew word for adversary became a title in God's court. Greek translators rendered it slanderer. By the time of the New Testament, Satan and the devil were names for one leader of evil.

words.d: the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun around the 200s BCE
from the Greek diabolos, slanderer; in the New Testament a name for Satan

look.title: All the Names at Once
look.text: And the great dragon was cast out, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world: he was cast out into the earth, and his angels were cast out with him.
look.prompt: List every name this verse gives the figure. Which one points back to Genesis 3?

check.q: What does the Greek word diabolos mean?
check.why: Diabolos means slanderer. The Septuagint used it for ha-satan in Job, and it gave English the word devil.

check.q: Which verse calls one figure the dragon, the old serpent, the devil and Satan?
check.why: Revelation 12:9 gathers all these names for one figure who deceives the whole world.

check.q: What is the Septuagint?
choices: The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible
A scroll of Enoch found near the Dead Sea
check.why: The Septuagint is the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun around the 200s BCE.

lessons.title: The Serpent in Eden
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 3 calls the tempter only "the serpent"; later writings link it to the devil, and readers still differ on what it was.
reading: Genesis 3 tells of a serpent in the garden of Eden. It speaks to the woman and questions God's command. The Hebrew word for serpent is *nachash*. Genesis 3 never calls it Satan. It is simply the serpent, more crafty than any creature God had made.

Heiser argued in The Unseen Realm (2015) that Eden was more than a garden. He read it as God's home on earth, where God met with his council. So he saw the serpent as a divine being, not just an animal. He noted that nachash is related to Hebrew words for shining and for divination. To him this hinted at a bright, heavenly figure.

In Heiser's reading, this being rebelled against God's plan for humans. His punishment was to be cast down to the ground, below the heavenly realm. Heiser called him the Eden *rebel*, and he saw him as the one the New Testament names Satan and the devil.

Other readers differ. Many Jewish readers treat the serpent as a clever animal in a story about human choices. An early link to the devil appears in the Wisdom of Solomon, a Jewish book written in Greek before the New Testament. Many Christians, following Revelation 12:9 and Romans 16:20, identify the serpent with Satan, as Heiser did, though not always for his reasons.

words.d: the Hebrew word for serpent in Genesis 3
one who rises up against a rightful ruler; Heiser's term for the serpent who turned against God in Eden

look.title: Through Envy of the Devil
look.text: Nevertheless through envy of the devil came death into the world
look.cite: Wisdom of Solomon 2:24, King James Version, Apocrypha (1611)
look.prompt: Genesis 3 never uses the word devil. Which story is this verse most likely pointing back to, and what does it add?

check.q: What Hebrew word does Genesis 3 use for the serpent?
check.why: Nachash is the Hebrew word for serpent in Genesis 3. Satan means adversary and diabolos is Greek for slanderer.

check.q: How did Heiser picture Eden?
choices: As a desert where Azazel lived
As a garden with no spirit beings in it
As God's home on earth where he met his council
As a city built by the king of Tyre
check.why: In The Unseen Realm (2015) Heiser read Eden as God's dwelling where his council met, so the serpent was a divine being.

check.q: Which early Jewish book says death came into the world through the envy of the devil?
check.why: Wisdom of Solomon 2:24, written in Greek before the New Testament, says death came into the world through the envy of the devil.

lessons.title: The King of Babylon
lessons.mainIdea: Isaiah 14 is a taunt song against the king of Babylon, who is pictured as a shining star thrown down from heaven.
reading: Isaiah 14:4 tells Israel to take up a taunt song against the king of Babylon. A *taunt song* mocks a proud enemy who has fallen. The poem imagines the dead in the underworld stirring to greet this king. They say he has become as weak as they are.

Isaiah 14:12 calls the king helel ben shachar in Hebrew. That means "shining one, son of the dawn", likely the morning star we now know as the planet Venus. Modern translations often say Day Star or morning star. The King James Version used *Lucifer*, a Latin word for the morning star meaning light-bringer.

In the poem, the king says in his heart that he will climb to heaven. He will set his throne above the stars of God and sit on the mount of assembly in the far north. He wants to be like the Most High. Instead, he is brought down to the pit.

Scholars have noticed that this language fits old stories from Canaan and Ugarit. Those stories told of gods meeting on a mountain in the north. The poem borrows that picture of a heavenly council to show how far the proud king falls.

words.d: a poem that mocks a proud enemy who has been brought low
a Latin word for the morning star, meaning light-bringer; used in the KJV at Isaiah 14:12

look.title: The Fallen Star
look.text: How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning! how art thou cut down to the ground, which didst weaken the nations!
look.prompt: Isaiah 14:4 says this poem is about the king of Babylon. What words in this verse picture him as a star?

check.q: According to Isaiah 14:4, who is the taunt song about?
check.why: Isaiah 14:4 says to take up this taunt song against the king of Babylon.

check.q: What does the Hebrew helel ben shachar mean?
choices: Shining one, son of the dawn
check.why: Helel ben shachar means shining one, son of the dawn, likely the morning star. The KJV used the Latin Lucifer.

check.q: Where does the king in the poem want to sit?
choices: In the garden of Eden by the river
On the mount of assembly in the far north
In the wilderness with a goat
At the gate of Tyre by the sea
check.why: Isaiah 14:13 has the king boast that he will sit on the mount of assembly in the far north, above the stars of God.

lessons.title: The King of Tyre
lessons.mainIdea: Ezekiel 28 speaks to the king of Tyre as if he had been a glorious being in Eden who fell through pride.
reading: Tyre was a rich port city on the coast of what is now Lebanon. Its merchants traded across the Mediterranean Sea. Around the 580s BCE, the prophet Ezekiel spoke against its king. In Ezekiel 28:2 the king claims to be a god, sitting in the seat of the gods. Ezekiel answers that he is only a man.

Then, in 28:12–19, Ezekiel sings a *lament*, a sad poem for the dead or the fallen. He says the king was in Eden, the garden of God. He was covered with precious stones. He is called an anointed *cherub* on the holy mountain of God. He was blameless until wrong was found in him.
His heart grew proud because of his beauty. His trade filled him with violence. So God cast him from the mountain of God to the ground. The poem ends with the king as a warning to other rulers.

The lament mixes two pictures. One is a real king growing rich through trade. The other is a shining being in Eden who is thrown down. Readers have argued for centuries about how these two pictures fit together.

words.d: a sad poem or song, often mourning a death or a fall
a winged heavenly guardian in the Hebrew Bible, like those who guard Eden in Genesis 3:24

look.title: A King in Eden
look.text: Paraphrase of Ezekiel 28:13–17: You were in Eden, the garden of God, covered with precious stones. You were an anointed cherub on God's holy mountain. You were blameless until wrong was found in you. Your heart grew proud because of your beauty, so I threw you to the ground.
look.prompt: Which details fit a human king of a trading city? Which details sound like a being from God's heavenly court?

check.q: Who is Ezekiel's lament in chapter 28 about?
check.why: Ezekiel 28:12 directs the lament to the king of Tyre, a rich trading city on the coast.

check.q: In Ezekiel 28, why is the king thrown down?
choices: He refused to count his people
His heart grew proud because of his beauty
He wore dirty clothes before God
He built a tower in Babylon
check.why: Ezekiel 28:17 says the king's heart grew proud because of his beauty, so God cast him to the ground.

check.q: What is a cherub in the Hebrew Bible?
check.why: A cherub is a heavenly guardian. Cherubim guard the way to the tree of life in Genesis 3:24.

lessons.title: Kings or a Fallen Spirit?
lessons.mainIdea: Readers see Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28 as poems about human kings, about a fallen spirit, or about kings pictured through an older story of a rebel cast down.
reading: Many Jewish readers and many modern scholars read both poems as being about human kings. Isaiah names Babylon; Ezekiel names Tyre. In their view, the heavenly language is poetry. It shows how high these kings raised themselves and how far they fell.

Many Christian readers, from early church writers such as Origen and Tertullian onward, also saw the fall of a spirit being in these poems. They read them as telling how Satan fell through pride. That is why the name Lucifer, from Isaiah 14, became a popular name for the devil.

Heiser took a middle path in The Unseen Realm (2015). He agreed that the poems are aimed at real human kings. But he argued they borrow the story of a divine rebel who was cast down. For Heiser, the pattern behind both poems was the rebel of *Eden*: a shining being who wanted to rise, and fell.
All three readings take the words seriously. They differ on how poetry works and on what the poets had in mind. A careful reader can explain each view and point to the verses each one leans on.

words.d: the garden of God in Genesis 2–3; Ezekiel 28:13 also names it
a reader's explanation of what a text means

look.title: Origen on the Prince of Tyre
look.text: Origen asks how anyone could think the words about the prince of Tyre were spoken of a mere man, since they place him in Eden as a cherub. He reads Isaiah's fallen morning star as a being who once shone in heaven and then fell.
look.cite: Origen, On First Principles 1.5.4–5, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 4 (1885), paraphrased
look.prompt: Which details from Ezekiel 28 does Origen's reading lean on? How would a reader who sees only a human king answer him?

check.q: How do many Jewish readers and modern scholars read Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28?
choices: As laws for the Day of Atonement
As prayers of the high priest
check.why: Many read both as poems about real kings of Babylon and Tyre, with heavenly language used as poetry.

check.q: Which early Christian writer read the poem about the prince of Tyre as more than a human king?
check.why: In On First Principles, Origen argued the words about the prince of Tyre could not fit a mere man and read them as the fall of a spirit being.

check.q: Why did Lucifer become a popular name for the devil?
choices: The Hebrew Bible uses it as Satan's name in Job
Ezekiel calls the king of Tyre Lucifer
Jesus uses the name in the Gospels
Christian readers linked Isaiah 14 to Satan's fall
check.why: Many Christian readers read Isaiah 14:12 as Satan's fall, so the KJV's word Lucifer became a name for the devil.

lessons.title: Belial and Mastema
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish writings from the Second Temple period gave the leader of evil spirits new names, such as Belial and Mastema.
reading: The *Second Temple period* runs from about 516 BCE, when the temple was rebuilt, to 70 CE, when the Romans destroyed it. In these centuries Jewish writers wrote many books outside the Hebrew Bible. Some of them gave names to a leader of evil powers.

One name is *Belial*. In the Hebrew Bible, beliyya'al is a word meaning worthlessness. The KJV prints phrases like "sons of Belial" for wicked men, as in 1 Samuel 2:12. In the Dead Sea Scrolls, Belial becomes a leader of evil. The War Scroll describes a coming battle of the sons of light against the sons of darkness, who belong to Belial.

Another name is *Mastema*, from a Hebrew word for hostility. The book of Jubilees, written around 160 BCE, calls him the chief of the spirits. In Jubilees 10, Noah prays against the evil spirits troubling his grandchildren. Mastema asks God to leave some spirits under his control. God allows a tenth to stay and binds the rest.

Paul uses the name Belial once. In 2 Corinthians 6:15 he asks what agreement Christ could have with Belial. Elaine Pagels, in The Origin of Satan (1995), is one of many scholars who trace how Jewish thinking about a chief enemy grew in these centuries.

words.d: the years from the rebuilding of the temple (about 516 BCE) to its destruction by Rome (70 CE)
from a Hebrew word for worthlessness; in the Dead Sea Scrolls, a name for the leader of evil
from a Hebrew word for hostility; in Jubilees, the chief of the evil spirits

look.title: How Long Ago? (Approximate)
look.cite: Common scholarly dates: Isaiah c. 700s BCE, Ezekiel c. 580s BCE, Zechariah c. 520 BCE, Jubilees c. 160 BCE, Revelation c. 95 CE
look.prompt: About how many years passed between Zechariah's visions and the writing of Jubilees? Why might ideas about the adversary change over that time?

check.q: Which book calls Mastema the chief of the spirits?
check.why: The book of Jubilees, written around 160 BCE, names Mastema as chief of the evil spirits.

check.q: In the Dead Sea Scrolls' War Scroll, who belongs to Belial?
choices: The sons of God in Job
check.why: The War Scroll describes the sons of light fighting the sons of darkness, who belong to Belial.

check.q: Where does Paul use the name Belial?
check.why: In 2 Corinthians 6:15 Paul asks what agreement Christ has with Belial.

lessons.title: Satan in the Gospels
lessons.mainIdea: In the Gospels, Satan and the devil are names for one enemy who tests Jesus and whose power Jesus says is ending.
reading: The Gospels of Matthew, Mark and Luke all tell of Jesus being tested in the wilderness. In Matthew 4:1–11 the devil offers him bread, a leap from the temple and all the kingdoms of the world. Jesus answers each time with words from Deuteronomy. The devil leaves.

Notice the offer of kingdoms. In Luke 4:6 the devil claims that authority over the kingdoms has been given to him. Some scholars read this against Deuteronomy 32, where the nations were placed under other heavenly powers. Other readers see it as the devil's boast, not a true claim.

In Luke 10:18, when his followers return from their mission, Jesus says he saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven. In John 12:31 he calls the devil the *ruler of this world* and says he will be cast out. The New Testament pictures Satan as a real enemy whose power is being broken.

Revelation 12 then shows a war in heaven. Michael and his angels fight the dragon, who is thrown down to the earth. Many readers see the New Testament gathering the threads of the Old: the serpent, the accuser and the fallen king. It gives them one name.

words.d: Jesus's title for the devil in John 12:31, pointing to his claimed power over the world
a test that pulls someone toward doing wrong

check.why: John 12:31 calls him the ruler of this world and says he will be cast out. Chief of the spirits is Jubilees' title for Mastema.

review.q: Which word best translates the Hebrew satan?

review.q: In which two books does "the satan" act as an accuser in God's court?

review.q: The KJV word Lucifer in Isaiah 14:12 comes from which language?
review.why: Lucifer is a Latin word for the morning star, meaning light-bringer. The Hebrew is helel ben shachar.

review.q: Which poem says the king was in Eden, the garden of God?
choices: Isaiah 14, about the king of Babylon
Job 1, about the court of God
Ezekiel 28, about the king of Tyre

chapters.title: Where Do Demons Come From?
chapters.bigQuestion: Where did ancient Jewish and Christian writers think unclean spirits came from, and how do their answers shape the way the Gospels are read?

story.title: The Man Who Ran to the Shore
story.kicker: On the far side of the Sea of Galilee, a man who has lived alone for a long time runs toward a boat.
paragraphs: The Gospel of Mark tells of a boat crossing the Sea of Galilee at night. Jesus and his followers land on the eastern shore, in the country of the Gerasenes. Most people there were not Jewish. On the hillside above the water, a large herd of pigs is feeding.

Near the shore are tombs cut into the rock. Mark says a man lived there, away from his town. People had tried to hold him with chains, but he broke them. Day and night he cried out among the tombs and the hills. The people of his town had stopped coming near.

Then Mark adds a surprising detail. When the man sees Jesus from far off, he does not run away. He runs toward him and kneels. Mark says an unclean spirit was troubling the man. Jesus speaks to it and asks its name. It answers, Legion, for we are many.

By the end of the story, the man is sitting calmly, dressed, next to Jesus. He asks to get into the boat and go along. Jesus says no. He tells him to go home to his own people and tell them what the Lord has done for him. The man goes through the Ten Cities, telling his story.

Readers have asked many questions about stories like this one. What did people in Jesus's time think these spirits were? Where did they come from? One very old answer comes from an ancient Jewish book called 1 Enoch. This chapter reads that answer and others, what scholars have made of them, and how to read these stories with care.
story.think: The story ends with the man going home to his own people. Why might Mark end the story there instead of with him leaving in the boat?

lessons.title: Three Stories of Rebellion
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis tells three stories of rebellion, and some scholars link each one to a different kind of dark power.
reading: Many people use the words Satan, fallen angels and demons as if they meant the same thing. The ancient texts are more varied than that. Start with Genesis. It tells three stories in which the order God set up is broken. Readers often call them the three *rebellions* of Genesis.

The first rebellion is in Eden, Genesis 3, where the serpent turns humans away from God. The second is Genesis 6:1–4, where the sons of God take human wives and the Nephilim, or giants, are born. The third is Babel, Genesis 11, when God scatters the nations.

Michael Heiser, in Demons (2020), linked each story to a group of dark powers. First is the Eden rebel, whom the New Testament calls the devil. Second are the sons of God set over the nations, who became corrupt. Paul's letters call powers like these *principalities*, or rulers. Third are *demons*, which he read as the spirits of the dead giants.
Not every scholar sorts things this way. Many Christian teachers treat all these as one group of fallen angels led by Satan. Heiser's map is one way to organize the texts this chapter reads next.

words.d: acts of rising up against a rightful ruler; Genesis 3, 6 and 11 each tell one
an older English word for rulers; in Paul's letters, spiritual powers over the world
evil spirits; the Gospels also call them unclean spirits

look.title: One Scholar's Map
look.text: Genesis 3, Eden: the serpent rebels. Group: the devil, or Satan. Genesis 6, the sons of God and the giants: Group: demons, the giants' spirits. Genesis 11, Babel: the nations are scattered under other sons of God. Group: principalities, the rulers over nations.
look.prompt: Explain this map in your own words. Which rebellion goes with which group, and which texts would you check first?

check.q: Which three Genesis chapters tell stories of rebellion?
check.why: Genesis 3 tells of Eden, Genesis 6 of the sons of God and the giants, and Genesis 11 of Babel.

check.q: In Heiser's reading, what are demons?
choices: The spirits of the dead giants
The rulers set over the nations
check.why: Heiser read demons as the spirits of the giants, the Nephilim, born in the Genesis 6 story.

check.q: How do many Christian teachers group these dark powers?
choices: As powers that appear only in Job
As spirits named in the Septuagint only
As three kinds of human kings
As one group of fallen angels led by Satan
check.why: Many Christian teachers treat all dark powers as fallen angels led by Satan, rather than as three groups.

lessons.title: Rulers Over the Nations
lessons.mainIdea: Deuteronomy 32 and Paul's letters speak of spirit powers over nations, and scholars differ on who Paul's rulers and powers are.
reading: Deuteronomy 32:8, in the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Septuagint, says God divided the nations by the number of the sons of God. Many scholars read this to mean God placed the nations under lesser heavenly beings. Israel stayed God's own portion. You met this reading in the unit on the gods of the nations.

A few verses later, Deuteronomy 32:17 says Israel sacrificed to *shedim*, not to God. Shedim is a Hebrew word for spirit beings. It is related to a word in Akkadian, the language of ancient Mesopotamia. The Greek Septuagint translated it daimonia, demons. The KJV says "devils".

Daniel 10 speaks of a prince of Persia and a prince of Greece who resist a heavenly messenger. Paul, writing in Greek, uses words like rulers, authorities and powers. Ephesians 6:12 says the struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and powers of darkness in the heavenly places.

Scholars read Paul's powers in different ways. Some see the sons of God of Deuteronomy 32, who turned corrupt, as Psalm 82 describes. Clinton E. Arnold, in Powers of Darkness (1992), read them as real spirit beings opposed to God. Walter Wink, in Naming the Powers (1984), argued they have an inner spiritual side and an outer side in human institutions.

words.d: a Hebrew word for spirit beings, used in Deuteronomy 32:17; the Septuagint translated it demons
in Paul's letters, a word for spiritual rulers or authorities

look.title: Sacrifices to Shedim
look.text: They sacrificed unto devils, not to God; to gods whom they knew not, to new gods that came newly up, whom your fathers feared not.
look.prompt: The KJV word "devils" translates the Hebrew shedim. How does the verse describe these beings? What does it say they are not?

check.q: What Hebrew word in Deuteronomy 32:17 names the spirit beings Israel sacrificed to?
check.why: Deuteronomy 32:17 uses shedim. The Septuagint translated it daimonia, and the KJV says devils.

check.q: Which verse says the struggle is against rulers and powers, not flesh and blood?
check.why: Ephesians 6:12 says the struggle is against rulers and powers of darkness in the heavenly places.

check.q: How did Walter Wink read Paul's powers in Naming the Powers (1984)?
choices: As the spirits of the dead giants
As Roman soldiers and nothing more
As the priests of the temple
As having a spiritual side and an outer side in human institutions
check.why: Wink argued that the powers have an inner spiritual side and an outer side in human institutions. Clinton Arnold read them as real spirit beings.

lessons.title: Unclean Spirits
lessons.mainIdea: The Gospels call demons unclean spirits, using a word from Israel's laws about what may come near God's holy presence.
reading: The Gospel of Mark often uses the phrase *unclean spirit*. In Greek it is pneuma akatharton. Mark also uses daimonion, *demon*, for the same beings. The KJV usually translates daimonion as "devil", so it can say Jesus cast out many devils. Modern translations usually say demons.

Why unclean? In the Law of Moses, being unclean did not mean being dirty or bad. It meant not being ready to come near God's holy presence. Touching a dead body made a person unclean for a time, as Numbers 19 says. Certain animals, like pigs, were unclean to eat. There were ways to become clean again.

Scholars have noticed how many unclean things fill the story of the man from the tombs. The tombs held the dead. The land was outside Israel. A herd of pigs fed nearby. In that setting, Mark says an unclean spirit troubled the man, and Jesus set him free.

So the name tells readers something. In the Gospels, these spirits stand against God's holy presence. Jesus, in the stories, has authority over them. That is why Mark tells the story of the man from the tombs the way he does.

words.d: the Gospels' phrase for a demon; unclean means not fit to come near God's holy presence
from the Greek daimonion; an evil spirit in the New Testament, often called "devil" in the KJV

look.title: Clean and Unclean
look.text: In the Law of Moses, a person who touched a dead body was unclean for seven days and then washed to become clean again (Numbers 19:11–12). Pigs were unclean animals to eat (Leviticus 11:7). In Mark 5, a man lives among tombs, in a land outside Israel, near a herd of pigs.
look.prompt: Why might Mark's first readers notice the unclean things in this setting? What does the story show Jesus doing in that place?

check.q: In the Law of Moses, what did "unclean" mean?
choices: Not ready to come near God's holy presence
check.why: Unclean meant not fit to come near God's holy presence for a time. Laws such as Numbers 19 showed how to become clean again.

check.q: How does the KJV usually translate the Greek daimonion?
check.why: The KJV usually renders daimonion as devil, as in cast out many devils. Modern translations usually say demon.

check.q: Which detail from Mark 5 is NOT one of the unclean things in the setting?
check.why: The tombs, the pigs and the land outside Israel were all unclean under the Law. The boat was not.

lessons.title: What 1 Enoch 15 Says
lessons.mainIdea: 1 Enoch 15 says that when the giants died, their spirits went out as evil spirits on the earth.
reading: *1 Enoch* is an ancient Jewish book, written in parts between about 300 BCE and the time of Jesus. Pieces of it in Aramaic were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. J. T. Milik published them in 1976. The full book survives in Ge'ez, the old language of Ethiopia. It is part of the Bible only in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches.

Its first part, the Book of the *Watchers*, retells Genesis 6. In 1 Enoch, the Watchers are heavenly beings who came down to earth, took human wives and fathered giants. The giants brought violence, and God sent judgment. In chapters 12–16, the Watchers ask Enoch to plead for them, and God gives Enoch a reply.

In 1 Enoch 15:8–12, God explains what happens to the giants. They were born from spirits and flesh. So when their bodies die, the spirits that come out of them will be called evil spirits on the earth. The earth will be their home. They will trouble people, because they came from people.

This is one of the earliest explanations of evil spirits that survives. It appears in a Jewish book that many people read in the centuries before the Gospels were written. Many scholars think it helps explain why the Gospels speak of unclean spirits so often.

words.d: an ancient Jewish book about Enoch and the Watchers, canonical in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches
in 1 Enoch, heavenly beings who came down, took human wives and fathered giants

look.title: The Giants' Spirits
look.text: The giants were born from spirits and from flesh. So they will be called evil spirits upon the earth, and the earth will be where they live. Evil spirits have come out of their bodies.
look.cite: 1 Enoch 15:8–9, after R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch (1917) (paraphrased)
look.prompt: According to this passage, why do the giants' spirits stay on the earth instead of going to heaven?

check.q: According to 1 Enoch 15, what happens when the giants' bodies die?
choices: They rise to heaven as angels
Their spirits become evil spirits on the earth
They become stars in the sky
They turn into the Rephaim kings
check.why: 1 Enoch 15:8–9 says the spirits that come out of the giants will be called evil spirits and will live on the earth.

check.q: Which churches include 1 Enoch in their Bible?
choices: The Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches
check.why: 1 Enoch is canonical only in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches.

check.q: Who asks Enoch to plead for them in 1 Enoch 12–16?
check.why: In 1 Enoch the Watchers ask Enoch to plead with God for them, and God sends back a reply of judgment.

lessons.title: From Enoch to the Gospels
lessons.mainIdea: Many scholars think 1 Enoch's story of the giants' spirits shaped how Jewish readers of Jesus's day understood unclean spirits.
reading: The Hebrew Bible says little about demons like those in the Gospels. Then, in the Gospels, unclean spirits appear often. Where did the idea come from? Many researchers point to the Book of the Watchers and to other books that retell it.

The evidence starts with the documents. Copies of 1 Enoch were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, so the book was read in the *Second Temple* period. Jubilees 10 retells the story, with evil spirits troubling Noah's grandchildren. The New Testament knows 1 Enoch too: Jude 14–15 quotes it by name.

Archie T. Wright, in The Origin of Evil Spirits (2005), studied how early Jewish writers received the Genesis 6 story. He traced how the giants' spirits became a way to explain evil spirits. Loren Stuckenbruck, in The Myth of Rebellious Angels (2014), also studied these traditions. Michael Heiser made the same link for general readers in Demons (2020).

Scholars offer this link as the best explanation of the *evidence*, not the only one. The Gospels themselves never say where demons come from. The link rests on reading them alongside the Jewish books their first readers knew.

words.d: the period from about 516 BCE to 70 CE, when Jerusalem's second temple stood
facts or texts that support an argument

look.title: The Five Parts of 1 Enoch
look.cite: The standard five-part division of 1 Enoch, as in R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch (1917)
look.prompt: Chapter 15 falls in which part? Which part is the longest, and which is the shortest?

check.q: Which New Testament book quotes 1 Enoch by name?
check.why: Jude 14–15 quotes a prophecy of Enoch, which matches 1 Enoch 1:9.

check.q: Which fact shows that 1 Enoch was read before the Gospels were written?
choices: The Gospels say plainly where demons come from
Leviticus names the giants as demons
Copies of it were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls
check.why: Copies of 1 Enoch among the Dead Sea Scrolls show it was read in the Second Temple period. The Gospels themselves do not give an origin.

check.q: In which part of 1 Enoch is chapter 15?
check.why: The Book of the Watchers covers chapters 1–36, so chapter 15 is in it.

lessons.title: Other Answers
lessons.mainIdea: Many Christians have taught that demons are fallen angels, while other ancient writers held views close to 1 Enoch's.
reading: A common Christian view says demons are *fallen angels* themselves. On this view, when Satan rebelled, some angels joined him. Readers point to Revelation 12:9, which says the dragon's angels were thrown down with him. Matthew 25:41 also speaks of the devil and his angels.

Other early Christians held views close to 1 Enoch's. Justin Martyr, a Christian writer around 150 CE, wrote about this in his Second Apology. He said angels fathered children with women, and that these children are the ones called demons. So the 1 Enoch reading has ancient company.

Jewish writings give still more accounts. The book of *Jubilees*, from about 160 BCE, tells of evil spirits that trouble Noah's grandchildren. God binds nine-tenths of them and leaves one-tenth under Mastema. Later rabbis wrote about spirits in many different ways.

The Jewish historian Josephus, writing in the 70s CE, gives yet another view. In Jewish War 7.6.3 he says that what people called demons were the spirits of wicked people who had died. The texts do not agree. Readers can weigh each view by the passages it uses.

words.d: angels who, in many Christian teachings, joined Satan's rebellion against God
a Jewish book from about 160 BCE that retells Genesis and early Exodus

look.title: Justin on the Angels' Children
look.text: Justin says God gave the care of people to angels. But the angels broke this order, loved women and fathered children. Those children, he says, are the ones called demons.
look.cite: Justin Martyr, Second Apology, chapter 5, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1 (1885), paraphrased
look.prompt: Which story from Genesis 6 and 1 Enoch does Justin retell? How does his view differ from the view that demons are fallen angels?

check.q: Which verse do readers use to say demons are fallen angels?
choices: Revelation 12:9, where the dragon's angels are thrown down
check.why: Revelation 12:9 says the dragon's angels were thrown down with him, which supports the fallen-angel view.

check.q: Which early Christian writer said demons were the children of angels and women?
check.why: Justin Martyr, around 150 CE, wrote that angels fathered children with women and those children are called demons.

check.q: In Jubilees, how many of the evil spirits are left under Mastema?
check.why: In Jubilees 10 God binds nine-tenths of the spirits and leaves one-tenth under Mastema.

lessons.title: In the Synagogue at Capernaum
lessons.mainIdea: Mark's first story of Jesus's work shows him freeing a man from an unclean spirit with a word, and the crowd amazed at his authority.
reading: Capernaum was a fishing town on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee. Mark 1:21–28 says Jesus taught there in the *synagogue*, a Jewish meeting place for prayer and study, on the Sabbath. The people were amazed. He taught with authority, not like the scribes.

Then a man with an unclean spirit cried out. The spirit asked what Jesus wanted with them, and called him the Holy One of God. Jesus told it to be silent and come out. Mark says the spirit shook the man, cried out and left him.

The crowd's question is the point of the story. They asked what this new teaching was, since even unclean spirits obeyed him. News about Jesus spread through all of Galilee. Mark puts this story near the start of his Gospel. It sets up Jesus's *authority* as a main theme.

Some readers see these stories as part of a larger picture. In that view, Jesus came to take back what the dark powers had claimed. Other readers focus on what the story shows about Jesus's teaching or about the man. All agree that Mark wants readers to ask who Jesus is.

words.d: a Jewish meeting place for prayer, reading and study
the right and power to give commands that others obey

look.title: The Crowd Wonders
look.text: What thing is this? what new doctrine is this? for with authority commandeth he even the unclean spirits, and they do obey him.
look.prompt: What two things amaze the crowd? Why might Mark place their question at the very start of his Gospel?

check.q: Where does the story in Mark 1:21–28 take place?
choices: Among the tombs of the Gerasenes
check.why: Mark 1:21 says Jesus taught in the synagogue at Capernaum on the Sabbath.

check.q: What amazed the crowd in Mark 1:27?
choices: Even unclean spirits obeyed Jesus's word
Jesus sailed across the sea at night
check.why: The crowd asked what this new teaching was, since Jesus commanded even unclean spirits with authority.

check.q: What does the unclean spirit call Jesus?
check.why: In Mark 1:24 the spirit calls Jesus the Holy One of God.

lessons.title: The Man from the Tombs
lessons.mainIdea: In Mark 5 Jesus frees a man near the tombs and sends him home to his own people to tell his story.
reading: Mark 5:1–20 is set in the country of the Gerasenes, east of the Sea of Galilee. A man lived among the tombs, apart from his town. When he saw Jesus, he ran and knelt before him. Jesus asked the spirit's name. It answered *Legion*, the word for a Roman army unit of thousands, "for we are many."

The spirits asked to be sent into a herd of pigs on the hillside. Jesus allowed it. Mark says about two thousand pigs rushed down the steep bank into the sea. The herders ran to tell the town. When people came, they found the man sitting with Jesus, dressed and calm.

The townspeople were afraid and asked Jesus to leave. The man begged to go with him. Jesus said no. He sent the man home to his friends, to tell them what the Lord had done and how he had shown him mercy. The man told his story in the *Decapolis*, the Ten Cities, and people were amazed.

The story ends with a person back among his people. He has a home, friends and a town. Instead of being avoided, he is the one telling the news. The people who once stayed away now come to hear what happened to him.

words.d: a Roman army unit of several thousand soldiers; the name the spirit gives in Mark 5:9
Greek for Ten Cities; a group of mostly non-Jewish towns east of the Sea of Galilee

look.title: Go Home
look.text: Howbeit Jesus suffered him not, but saith unto him, Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee.
look.prompt: "Suffered him not" means "did not let him". What does Jesus not let the man do, and what does he send him to do instead?

check.q: What does the name Legion refer to?
choices: A town in the Ten Cities
A Roman army unit of thousands
A book of the Dead Sea Scrolls
check.why: A legion was a Roman army unit of several thousand, which fits the answer "for we are many" in Mark 5:9.

check.q: What did Jesus tell the man to do in Mark 5:19?
choices: Get into the boat and follow him
Go home to his friends and tell them what the Lord had done
Stay among the tombs and wait
Travel to Jerusalem to see the priests
check.why: Mark 5:19 says Jesus sent him home to his friends to tell how the Lord had shown him mercy.

check.q: Where did the man tell his story?
choices: In the Decapolis, the Ten Cities
In the court of the king of Tyre
check.why: Mark 5:20 says he told what Jesus had done for him throughout the Decapolis.

lessons.title: Reading These Stories With Care
lessons.mainIdea: The Gospels treat healing the sick and freeing people from spirits as different things, and they end these stories with people restored to their communities.
reading: Read Mark 1:32–34 closely. At sunset, people bring to Jesus those who were sick and those troubled by demons. Mark then says he healed many who were sick with various diseases and cast out many demons. Mark lists these as two separate groups. Matthew 4:24 does the same.

This matters for how the stories are read today. Illness, disability and differences in how people's minds work are a normal part of human life. They are never a sign of an evil spirit, and no one should ever be treated that way. The Gospel writers themselves kept healing and freeing apart.

Look also at how the stories end. The man in Capernaum is freed right in his own town's synagogue. The man from the tombs goes home to his friends. In Mark 5:34 a woman who is healed is called daughter. The people in these stories have names, homes and families. The stories end with *restoration*: a person welcomed back.
This course studies how these texts were read. It does not teach any spiritual practice. Readers from many backgrounds notice two things in these stories: Jesus's authority and his care for people.

words.d: bringing someone or something back to a good and whole state
a group of people who live together and belong to one another

look.title: Two Groups in One Verse
look.text: Paraphrase of Mark 1:32–34: That evening, after sunset, people brought to Jesus all who were sick and all who were troubled by demons. The whole town gathered at the door. He healed many who had various diseases, and he cast out many demons.
look.prompt: How many different groups of people does this passage name? What does that tell you about how Mark saw sickness and spirits?

check.q: How does Mark 1:32–34 describe the people brought to Jesus?
choices: As one group, all troubled by spirits
As two separate groups: the sick and those troubled by demons
As soldiers from a Roman legion
check.why: Mark 1:32–34 names the sick and those troubled by demons as two groups, and says Jesus healed one and cast out the other.

check.q: How do the Gospel stories of freeing people usually end?
choices: With the person sent away from town
With the person hidden in the tombs
With the person restored to home and community
With the person forgotten by the writer
check.why: The stories end in restoration: the man from the tombs, for example, goes home to tell his friends.

check.q: Which statement fits how these stories should be read today?
choices: Illness, disability and different minds are never signs of an evil spirit
Matthew joins sickness and spirits into one group
The Gospels give steps for readers to follow
Healing and freeing mean the same thing in Mark
check.why: The Gospels keep healing and freeing apart, and illness, disability and different minds are part of human life, never a spirit.

sections.title: Azazel and the Day of Atonement

lessons.title: Two Goats
lessons.mainIdea: On the Day of Atonement, one goat was offered to the LORD and the other carried the people's sins into the wilderness, for Azazel.
reading: Leviticus 16 describes the *Day of Atonement*, Yom Kippur. Once a year, on the tenth day of the seventh month, the high priest entered the Most Holy Place. The day was set aside to make the people and the sanctuary clean before God. Jews still keep Yom Kippur today as a day of fasting and prayer.

The ceremony used two goats. The high priest cast lots over them. One lot was for the LORD, and the other was for *Azazel*. The goat for the LORD was offered as a sin offering. Its blood was used to cleanse the sanctuary.

Then the high priest laid both hands on the head of the living goat. He confessed over it all the sins of the people. A man led the goat away into the wilderness. Leviticus 16:22 says the goat carried the people's sins to a land cut off from people.

The picture is clear even to a first-time reader. The people's wrongs are not just forgiven. They are carried away, far from the camp, out of sight. Readers have long asked the same question: who or what is Azazel?

words.d: Yom Kippur, the yearly day in Leviticus 16 for cleansing the people and the sanctuary
the name in Leviticus 16:8 to which the second goat is sent; its meaning is debated

look.title: Leviticus 16 by the Numbers
rows: Rams (one for Aaron, one for the people)
look.prompt: Of the two goats, how many were offered on the altar? What happened to the other one?

check.q: What did the high priest do with the living goat before it was sent away?
choices: Laid his hands on it and confessed the people's sins
check.why: Leviticus 16:21 says he laid both hands on the living goat and confessed all the people's sins over it.

check.q: How were the two goats assigned?
choices: By casting lots, one for the LORD and one for Azazel
By color, the dark one for the LORD
By age, the older one for Azazel
check.why: Leviticus 16:8 says the high priest cast lots over the two goats: one for the LORD and one for Azazel.

check.q: When did the Day of Atonement fall?
choices: On the first day of the first month
On the tenth day of the seventh month
On the day of a new king
check.why: Leviticus 16:29 sets it on the tenth day of the seventh month, once a year.

lessons.title: Who Is Azazel?
lessons.mainIdea: Azazel has been read as the goat that goes away, as a rugged place and as a wilderness spirit; 1 Enoch makes Azazel a leader of the Watchers.
reading: The Greek Septuagint called the second goat the one "sent away". In 1530 the English translator William Tyndale read Azazel the same way, as "the goat that goes away". He made up a new word: *scapegoat*. The King James Version kept it. Today scapegoat means someone blamed for others' wrongs.

Some later rabbis read Azazel as the name of a place: a rough, steep cliff in the wilderness. The Talmud, in tractate Yoma, describes the goat being taken to a high rocky place. On this reading, Azazel names where the goat went.

1 Enoch gives Azazel a different role. In 1 Enoch 8, Azazel is one of the leaders of the Watchers. He taught people to make weapons and jewelry. In 1 Enoch 10:4–5, God tells the angel Raphael to bind Azazel and cast him into darkness in the desert, under rough, jagged rocks.

Many scholars read Azazel as a wilderness *spirit being*, as 1 Enoch does. Even so, they note that the goat was not a gift to Azazel. It carried the people's sins out of the holy camp. It sent them back to a wild place, far from God's presence.

words.d: Tyndale's 1530 word for the goat sent away in Leviticus 16; now someone blamed for others' wrongs
a being of the unseen world, such as an angel, rather than a human or animal

look.title: Azazel Bound
look.text: The Lord told Raphael to bind Azazel hand and foot and throw him into the darkness. Raphael was to make an opening in the desert and put him there, and to lay rough, jagged rocks over him.
look.cite: 1 Enoch 10:4–5, after R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch (1917) (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Leviticus 16 sends a goat into the wilderness, and 1 Enoch binds Azazel in the desert. Why might readers see a link between the two?

check.q: Who coined the English word scapegoat?
check.why: William Tyndale made up scapegoat in 1530 for the goat that goes away. The KJV kept his word.

check.q: In 1 Enoch 10, what happens to Azazel?
choices: He is sent to rule Babylon
Raphael binds him and casts him into darkness in the desert
He is forgiven and made a cherub
He becomes high priest of Israel
check.why: 1 Enoch 10:4–5 says Raphael binds Azazel and casts him into darkness in the desert under jagged rocks.

check.q: How do many scholars who read Azazel as a spirit understand the goat?
choices: It carried sins away to the wild place linked with evil, not as a gift to Azazel
It was a symbol of the king of Tyre
It was an offering to please Azazel
It was a name for a rocky cliff only
check.why: They read Azazel as a wilderness spirit, but say the goat was not offered to him. It removed the people's sins from the holy camp.

review.q: In Heiser's three groups, which one comes from the Babel story?
review.why: Heiser tied the rulers, or principalities, to the sons of God set over the scattered nations after Babel.

review.q: Which ancient book says the giants' spirits became evil spirits on the earth?
review.why: 1 Enoch 15:8–12 says the spirits that came out of the dead giants became evil spirits living on the earth.

review.q: Who wrote The Origin of Evil Spirits (2005), on how early Jewish writers read Genesis 6?
review.why: Archie T. Wright's 2005 book traced how the giants' spirits in the Watchers story became a way to explain evil spirits.

review.q: What does the common Christian view say demons are?
review.why: Many Christians teach that demons are angels who joined Satan's rebellion, citing Revelation 12:9 and Matthew 25:41.

review.q: What happens at the end of the story of the man from the tombs?
choices: He is sent into the wilderness like the goat
He becomes a priest in Jerusalem
He goes home and tells his story in the Ten Cities
He sails away with Jesus to Capernaum
review.why: In Mark 5:19–20 Jesus sends him home, and he tells what the Lord did for him in the Decapolis.

review.q: Why does Mark 1:32–34 matter for reading these stories with care?
choices: It says Jesus stayed away from the town
It gives steps for casting out spirits
It names the giants of Genesis 6
It lists the sick and those troubled by demons as separate groups
review.why: Mark 1:32–34 names the sick and the troubled as two groups, keeping healing and freeing apart.

review.q: Which reading of Azazel comes from the Talmud?
choices: A rough, steep place in the wilderness
review.why: Tractate Yoma in the Talmud reads Azazel as a rocky place. 1 Enoch makes Azazel a Watcher, and Tyndale read it as the goat that goes away.

review.q: What Greek word gives the New Testament word demon?
review.why: Demon comes from daimonion. Diabolos gives devil, Satanas is Satan, and pneuma means spirit.
